article.Citation/Title: Rothberg, R. L., Azhari, N., Haug, N. A., & Dakwar, E. (2021). Mystical-type experiences occasioned by ketamine mediate its impact on at-risk drinking: Results from a randomized, controlled trial. Journal of Psychopharmacology, 35(2), 150-158.
article.InterventionDescription: IV ketamine (0.71 mg/kg) or midazolam (0.025 mg/kg) infused over 52 minutes on a quit-day in week 2 of a 5-week motivational enhancement therapy program, NYSPI outpatient setting.

article.Citation/Title: This is a secondary mediation analysis of the RCT reported in Dakwar E, Levin F, Hart CL, et al. (2020) 'A single ketamine infusion combined with motivational enhancement therapy for alcohol use disorder: A randomized midazolam-controlled pilot trial.' Am J Psychiatry 177: 125-133 (same N=40 sample, NCT02539511). Eligible as a secondary analysis per the boundary-case rule; parent trial named here per instructions.
article.Year: Masthead shows 'Journal of Psychopharmacology 2021, Vol. 35(2) 150-158 © The Author(s) 2020', i.e. an online-first 2020 copyright with a 2021 print-issue year. Coded Year=2021 (issue year) per the request's Year field and the field rule to prefer issue year, with the 2020 online-first copyright noted here as the discrepancy.
article.Outcome: Primary outcome is explicitly named in Methods/'Drinking outcome measures': '"At-risk" drinking post-infusion was used as the primary outcome measure' (NIAAA-defined heavy-use threshold over the 3-week post-infusion window). Its reported effect, in Results/'Infusion effects': 'Ketamine decreased the odds of engaging in at-risk drinking by approximately five times (p<0.05)' via binary logistic robust regression — no exact OR/CI is printed for this specific model. Table 2 gives the underlying raw proportions (ketamine 4/17 = 23.5% vs midazolam 11/23 = 47.8% engaged in at-risk drinking), which is the numeric pairing recorded here alongside the article's own 'approximately five times' language. This is the study's own primary comparison, distinct from the mediation analysis (HMS/CADSS) that is the paper's stated aim — per the prompt's precedence rule, Outcome is the stated primary outcome/comparison, not the mediation result the abstract emphasizes.
article.SD: No test statistic, standard error, or confidence interval is printed for the binary logistic robust regression that produced the 'approximately five times' odds estimate — only 'p<0.05' is given (Results/'Infusion effects'). Coded '.' rather than fabricating a value.
article.SampleSize_NFinal: Table 2 shows the primary at-risk-drinking analysis was run on all N=40 randomized participants (23 midazolam + 17 ketamine). Results/'Post-infusion drinking' confirms: 'Post-infusion drinking behavior was recorded for all 40 participants.' This N differs from the N=35 used in the separate mediation analysis (3 missing HMS, 2 missing CADSS, per Results/'Participants'), which is not the analysis that produced Outcome.

MethodologyDescribedYN.note: All elements are described except a priori sample-size/power justification for the primary hypothesis: the only power-adjacent statement concerns power for a normality test ('our small sample size (n=40) would preclude an adequately powered statistical test for normality'), not a sample-size/power rationale for the N=40 design itself. Harms is met because the article explicitly states no AEs occurred, which counts as 'described' per the described-vs-present distinction.

article.BaseStatus: Participants met DSM-IV alcohol dependence criteria with defined heavy-use thresholds (>4 drinks/day males / >3 females, or weekly minimums) and averaged 6.6 drinks/day (Table 1), but the article reports no formal severity grading instrument (e.g., DSM-5 mild/moderate/severe symptom count). Coded '.' rather than inferring a severity band from drinks/day alone.
article.Age_Median: Table 1: total sample mean age 53.0 (SD 9.8) -> bracket '50+'.
article.RaceEthnicity_BIPOCPercent: Table 1 race percentages (Asian 5.4%, Black/African American 13.5%, White 70.3%, Multiracial 10.8%) sum to 100% but are computed over n=37 (2+5+26+4=37), not the full n=40 sample — implying 3 participants had unreported/missing race data. Non-white sum = Asian + Black + Multiracial = 5.4+13.5+10.8 = 29.7%, reported as-is from the article's own percentage base rather than recalculated against n=40.
article.Retention (%): Results/'Post-infusion drinking': 'Post-infusion drinking behavior was recorded for all 40 participants,' and Table 2 totals 23+17=40, matching the randomized N with no separately reported dropout for the primary analysis. Denominator is the randomized N (40) per the field rule; completers=40, giving 100%.
article.Comparator: Comparator=1 for the active-control arm, midazolam (0.025 mg/kg IV). Note: the Methods opening sentence describes the parent trial as '...randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial...' while the Abstract and Infusion-procedures sections both correctly identify midazolam as an 'active control' — an internal labeling inconsistency in the article itself. Coded based on the actual design (active comparator), not the inconsistent 'placebo-controlled' phrase.
article.Power: No a priori power calculation for the primary hypothesis is reported. Coded 1 because the article repeatedly discusses the small-sample limitation in terms that function as a power discussion: it explicitly ties n=40 to inadequate power for a normality test (Statistical analyses section) and flags 'a relatively small sample size' as a limitation warranting larger future studies (Limitations) — treated as the 'bare statement that the study was underpowered' the rule says counts as 1.
article.RecruitmentRepresentYN: Coded 0: sample was a treatment-seeking volunteer cohort recruited under fairly narrow exclusion criteria (excluded any other substance dependence, active depressive disorder, and past/current bipolar or psychotic disorders), i.e. a screened research sample rather than a broadly representative clinical population, as the Limitations section itself acknowledges ('unknown whether these results would generalize to a broader population of alcohol-dependent individuals with psychiatric comorbidity').
article.Followup in months: Study design combines a 5-week (~1.15-month) MET/monitoring program with phone follow-up 'at 1 and 3 months following the completion of the study' (Study design and procedures). Measuring from end of treatment, the longest reported horizon is the 3-month post-completion phone follow-up; the primary at-risk-drinking outcome itself is assessed over a shorter 3-week (21-day) post-infusion window nested within the 5-week program.
article.CessationMeasured: Coded 1 because '% Days abstinent' is reported as a distinct outcome (Table 3), which functions as a cessation-oriented measure alongside the partial-reduction measures (heavy drinking days, % heavy drinking days) that justify ReductionMeasured=1.
article.ArmScope: Coded 'pooled' because the no-AE statements cover both arms jointly: 'All participants tolerated study procedures without adverse events' (Participants) and 'No adverse events were reported as a result of either the ketamine or midazolam infusions' (Infusion effects) — values are not reported separately for the ketamine-exposed arm alone.
article.SafetyReported: Coded 'Y' (not silence) because the article makes an explicit, affirmative safety statement in two places (Participants section and Results/'Infusion effects') rather than simply omitting an AE discussion — this distinguishes 'assessed, none occurred' from 'never looked.'

config_proposal.measure: 23.5% vs 47.8% (Table 2: ketamine 4/17 vs midazolam 11/23 engaged in at-risk drinking post-infusion)
config_proposal.note: Article states ketamine 'decreased the odds of engaging in at-risk drinking by approximately five times (p<0.05)' via binary logistic robust regression but prints no exact OR, CI, or test statistic for that model. Table 2's raw 2x2 proportions give a directly computable OR of (11/12)/(4/13) ≈ 2.98 (odds of at-risk drinking ~3x higher for midazolam than ketamine) — lower than the model-based 'approximately five times' language, likely reflecting the difference between the unadjusted crosstab and the robust-regression estimate; this discrepancy is not resolved, only flagged. 'At-risk drinking' is an adverse/undesired outcome, so OR<1 favors ketamine; direction=-1 flips the natural sign so a positive converted effect size favors the psychedelic arm, consistent with other studies' effect-direction convention. Approx (not clean) because the exact model OR is never printed; measure and computed_or instead use the raw table proportions.
